  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking 
<br class="ltx_break">in
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are two key steps in the post-training of modern Language Models (LMs). A common problem is reward hacking, where the policy may exploit inaccuracies of the reward and learn an unintended behavior. Most previous works address this by limiting the policy update with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty towards a reference model. We propose a different framing: Train the LM in a way that biases policy updates towards regions in which the reward is more accurate. First, we derive a theoretical connection between the accuracy of a reward model and the flatness of an optimum at convergence. Gradient regularization (GR) can then be used to bias training to flatter regions and thereby maintain reward model accuracy. We confirm these results by showing that the gradient norm and reward accuracy are empirically correlated in RLHF. We then show that Reference Resets of the KL penalty implicitly use GR to find flatter regions with higher reward accuracy. We further improve on this by proposing to use explicit GR with an efficient finite-difference estimate. Empirically, GR performs better than a KL penalty across a diverse set of RL experiments with LMs. GR achieves a higher GPT-judged win-rate in RLHF, avoids overly focusing on the format in rule-based math rewards, and prevents hacking the judge in LLM-as-a-Judge math tasks.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Reinforcement Learning, Post-Training, Gradient Regularization, RLHF, Reasoning, RLVR, LLMs
</div>

style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_tikzmatrix_col ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 24.45 0) translate(-0.21,0) -1 0 7.56)" width="17.88"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S1.F1.pic1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">GR</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g></g></g></g></g></g></svg></span></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We argue that reward hacking often corresponds to exploiting sharp maxima in action space, as illustrated by the conceptual figure (left).
For example, an LLM judge may be confused and assign a high reward to a wrong answer with specific formatting.
In the LLM-as-a-Judge training run shown on the right, the increase in gradient norm coincides with reward hacking, resulting in true reward collapsing.
By using gradient norm regularization, we can prevent this issue and obtain a better model, as seen by the improved true reward.
The examples show Qwen2.5-0.5B models trained on GSM8K with a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct judge with access to the true answer.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a key part of the post-training of language models (LMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
In the case of RL from Human Feedback (RLHF) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, we use RL to align the behavior of LMs with human preferences, which we cannot easily represent with a rule-based reward.
In the case of RL from Verifiable Feedback (RLVR) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Havrilla et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambert et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, RL is used to improve the performance on tasks with verifiable rewards, such as mathematical reasoning or agentic tasks.
In RLHF, we use pairwise comparison data to train a reward model (RM), which then provides the reward estimates for policy updates.
In RLVR, we use a verifier such as a rule-based reward or another Large Language Model (LLM) to check if the model output matches the expected answer.
In both cases there is a desired behavior, corresponding to a desired true reward, which we try to approximate with the trained RM, rule-based reward, or LLM-as-a-judge reward.
We collectively refer to them as proxy rewards (PRs).
A key challenge of RL post-training is:
How can we ensure that when updating our policy with the PR, we actually improve the true reward, i.e., how can we ensure that our PR stays accurate as the policy changes throughout training?
One solution is to iteratively update the PR during training with new data from the current policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
As this can be costly, another option is to use a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to ensure the policy stays close to the initial model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
In practice, the KL penalty slows down training and may not even improve performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, leading to recent papers abandoning it for tasks with rule-based rewards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-4.5 Team et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
However, this risks reward hacking with reward models and LLM-as-a-judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We thus aim to modify the policy update such that the policy not only maximizes the PR, but also maximizes the PR accuracy, without constraining it to stay close to the initial policy.
We argue that reward hacking often corresponds to sharp optima of the PR and propose gradient regularization (GR) as a solution. We illustrate an overview in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S3" title="3 Accurate Proxy Rewards via Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 3</span></a>, we formalize this notion and show a theoretical connection between the flatness of an optimum and the PR accuracy at this optimum, as measured by the Bradley-Terry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bradley and Terry, 1952</a>, BT;)</cite> loss.
In <a href="#S4" title="4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4</span></a>, we show that this theoretical connection can be utilized to improve RLHF in practice. We leverage a recent method, Reference Resets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and demonstrate that it implicitly regularizes the gradient, providing a novel interpretation of this method. We empirically show this enables better RLHF performance on the TL;DR task.
In <a href="#S5" title="5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 5</span></a>, we propose a novel application of explicit gradient regularization to RL post-training.
We demonstrate that it outperforms baselines in RLHF tasks with reward models as well as rule-based and LLM-as-a-judge RLVR math tasks.
By using GR, we are able to train proficient LLM-as-a-Judge and RLHF models <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">completely replacing the standard KL penalty</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Reinforcement Learning</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">As is common in the RL post-training literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ahmadian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we consider an episode consisting of a single state <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, representing the prompt, and a single action <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>, representing the reply.
We denote the state set by <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> and the action set by <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> with parameters <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, we consider an autoregressive LM with conditional probability <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(a|s)=\prod_{t}\pi_{\phi}(\mathfrak{a}_{t}|s,\mathfrak{a}_{&lt;t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∏</mo><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝔞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝔞</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(a|s)=\prod_{t}\pi_{\phi}(\mathfrak{a}_{t}|s,\mathfrak{a}_{&lt;t})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>-th response token, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{a}_{&lt;t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔞</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{a}_{&lt;t}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the response tokens before <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{a}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{a}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the entire response.
We assume that there is a true reward function <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> and our goal is to maximize the return of the policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> on this reward <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{*}(\phi)=\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[R^{*}(s,a)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{*}(\phi)=\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[R^{*}(s,a)]</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, we do not have access to <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Instead, we use a proxy reward (PR) <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, and train the policy to maximize its return <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J(\phi,\theta)=\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(\phi,\theta)=\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]</annotation></semantics></math>.
To optimize the return we use REINFORCE policy gradient updates <span id="S2.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams, 1992</a>)</cite></span></p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E1Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\expect_{s\sim P(s),a\sim\pi_{\phi}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E1Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left[(\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)-b(s))\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a|s)\right]\,," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.170em">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left[(\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)-b(s))\nabla_{\phi}\log\pi_{\phi}(a|s)\right]\,,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(s)</annotation></semantics></math> is a baseline.
In this work, we use a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> called GRPO Done Right (Dr.GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, which removes normalization terms from GRPO.
As we do not do multiple updates per batch, Dr.GRPO simplifies to using REINFORCE with the baseline being the sample average over multiple actions drawn for the same state, i.e, <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(s)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widetilde{R}(s,a^{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(s)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widetilde{R}(s,a^{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{i}\sim\pi_{\phi}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{i}\sim\pi_{\phi}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>.
GRPO was originally presented with a KL penalty <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\phi};\pi_{\phi^{1}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\phi};\pi_{\phi^{1}})</annotation></semantics></math>, as commonly used in RLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
This KL-penalty, weighted by a hyper-parameter <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, is intended to keep the model close to the initial policy <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi^{1}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi^{1}}</annotation></semantics></math>, preventing reward hacking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, but is sometimes omitted in more recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-4.5 Team et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Proxy Rewards</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider three types of PRs:
Trained reward models <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>θ</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, rule based rewards <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\mathrm{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>R</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\mathrm{R}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and LLM-as-a-Judge rewards <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\mathrm{LM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>LM</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\mathrm{LM}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reward Models</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">(RMs) are commonly used in RLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christiano et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>)</cite> to represent complex preferences which are hard to turn into rule-based rewards.
They generally assume the Bradley-Terry (BT) model of preference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bradley and Terry, 1952</a>)</cite> where the probability <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> of preferring one option <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> over another option <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> is the logistic function <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})}</annotation></semantics></math> of the difference of the true reward for each action, i.e.,</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(a_{1}&gt;a_{0}\mid s)=\sigma\left(R^{*}(s,a_{1})-R^{*}(s,a_{0})\right)\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(a_{1}&gt;a_{0}\mid s)=\sigma\left(R^{*}(s,a_{1})-R^{*}(s,a_{0})\right)\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Pairs of responses <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{0},a_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{0},a_{1})</annotation></semantics></math> for each prompt <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> are collected from an initial model <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi^{1}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msup></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi^{1}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Human annotators then choose their preferred (winning) reply <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\mathrm{w}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\mathrm{w}}</annotation></semantics></math> and not preferred (losing) reply <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\mathrm{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\mathrm{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>, creating a dataset <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\{(s^{j},a_{\mathrm{w}}^{j},a_{\mathrm{l}}^{j})\}_{j=1}^{{N_{\mathrm{RM}}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>RM</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>w</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>RM</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RM}}=\{(s^{j},a_{\mathrm{w}}^{j},a_{\mathrm{l}}^{j})\}_{j=1}^{{N_{\mathrm{RM}}}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We can then use the BT assumption to train an RM <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\theta}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> with parameters <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\Theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\Theta</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing the cross-entropy loss based on the BT model:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S2.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S2.E3Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle-\expect_{(s,a_{\mathrm{w}},a_{\mathrm{l}})\sim P_{\pi_{\phi}}}[\log\sigma(R_{\theta}(s,a_{\mathrm{w}})-R_{\theta}(s,a_{\mathrm{l}}))]\,," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></msub></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle-\expect_{(s,a_{\mathrm{w}},a_{\mathrm{l}})\sim P_{\pi_{\phi}}}[\log\sigma(R_{\theta}(s,a_{\mathrm{w}})-R_{\theta}(s,a_{\mathrm{l}}))]\,,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.4" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\pi_{\phi}}=P(s)\pi_{\phi}(a_{0}|s)\pi_{\phi}(a_{1}|s)P(a_{1}&gt;a_{0}|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\pi_{\phi}}=P(s)\pi_{\phi}(a_{0}|s)\pi_{\phi}(a_{1}|s)P(a_{1}&gt;a_{0}|s)</annotation></semantics></math> is the probability of the <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s,a_{\mathrm{w}},a_{\mathrm{l}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s,a_{\mathrm{w}},a_{\mathrm{l}})</annotation></semantics></math> triplet under the policy <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>.
To train the RM we minimize <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi^{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi^{1})</annotation></semantics></math> and the expectation is replaced by the sample average from <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>RM</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RM}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Rule-Based Rewards</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Havrilla et al., 2024</a>)</cite> are deterministic checks whether a final answer matches the ground truth.
To encourage reasoning, and to allow a discrimination of a final answer against occurrences of the answer during reasoning, rule-based rewards typically require the answer to follow a specific format, for example using the LaTeX tag <code id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">\boxed{}</code> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite> or the HTML tags <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a>)</cite> <code id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">&lt;think&gt;...&lt;/think&gt;&lt;answer&gt;...&lt;/answer&gt;</code>.
Thus, oftentimes one reward term <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\mathrm{F}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>F</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\mathrm{F}}</annotation></semantics></math> checks whether the format matches and another reward term <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\mathrm{C}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>C</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\mathrm{C}}</annotation></semantics></math> checks for correctness, to give the rule-based reward <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{\mathrm{R}}=R^{\mathrm{C}}+R^{\mathrm{F}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>R</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>C</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>F</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{\mathrm{R}}=R^{\mathrm{C}}+R^{\mathrm{F}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLM-as-a-Judge</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> prompts an LLM and uses its textual output to check whether an answer is correct. Frequently designing a rule-based reward can be challenging due to many possible accurate solutions, e.g., the correctness of a proof or many equivalent ways to write a math answer.
Instead, prompting an LLM-as-a-Judge with a description of scoring criteria, the question, and the correct answer (if available) can allow us to capture solutions more robustly.
LLM-as-a-Judge can also allow for more complicated rewards with a combination of objective (e.g., correct reply) and subjective (e.g., clear reasoning) criteria.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Gradient Regularization (GR)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flat minima of a loss function <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\phi)</annotation></semantics></math> are connected to better generalization in supervised learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, i.e., a smaller difference between the population/test loss <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P(x,y)}[\ell(f_{\phi}(x),y)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P(x,y)}[\ell(f_{\phi}(x),y)]</annotation></semantics></math> and
its empirical approximation
on a finite training dataset <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, consisting of i.i.d. input-label pairs <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(x,y)\sim P(x,y)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(x,y)\sim P(x,y)</annotation></semantics></math>, for a loss function <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>.
A way to obtain flat minima is by regularizing the gradient norm of the objective <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., the squared Euclidean norm <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
Adding this term to our loss function, we need to calculate its gradient, which can be approximated with a parameter perturbation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karakida et al., 2023</a>)</cite></p>
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta_{\phi}\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}=\frac{\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi+\varepsilon\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi))-\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)}{\varepsilon}\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mi>ε</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta_{\phi}\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}=\frac{\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi+\varepsilon\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi))-\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)}{\varepsilon}\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">The model parameters are then updated as</p>
<table id="S2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi\leftarrow\phi-\eta\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)-\eta\frac{\gamma}{2}\Delta_{\phi}\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}\,," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mi>γ</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi\leftarrow\phi-\eta\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)-\eta\frac{\gamma}{2}\Delta_{\phi}\|\nabla_{\phi}\mathcal{L}(\phi)\|^{2}\,,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the learning rate and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyper-parameter controlling the strength of the GR and <math id="S2.SS3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of the parameter perturbation.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Accurate Proxy Rewards via Gradient Regularization</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem Formulation and Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As mentioned above, the goal of RL is to learn a policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> that maximizes the expected true reward <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As we do not have access to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> we instead have to use the PR <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math> to update our policy.
As the PR is generally an approximation of the true reward <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, it may be prone to reward hacking and we need to ensure that the PR stays accurate during training.
For PRs that have been trained or designed based on samples from an initial policy <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>, such as RMs in RLHF, the most common solution is to use a KL penalty <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> ensuring that the policy stays close to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and thus the PR stays accurate.
However, the KL penalty also limits how much the policy can learn.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.F2.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" height="116.76" overflow="visible" sharp</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Conceptual illustration of our theoretical argument: (left) Regularizing the gradient norm biases optimization toward flat basins in parameter space, and (right) under action-smoothness, a flat maximum makes <math id="S3.F2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>-close pairs unlikely to have a reward gap larger than <math id="S3.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. decreases the probability of overly sharp action pairs <math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{1},a_{2}:\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|\leq\delta,|\widetilde{R}(s,a_{1})-\widetilde{R}(s,a_{2})|&gt;K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{1},a_{2}:\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|\leq\delta,|\widetilde{R}(s,a_{1})-\widetilde{R}(s,a_{2})|&gt;K</annotation></semantics></math>.
Under the assumption of a Lipschitz-continuous true reward <math id="S3.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, each such pair implies an incorrect proxy reward <math id="S3.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo mathsize="1.110em">~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math>.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of changing the PR <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math> or constraining <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, we aim to update the policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> such that it obtains a high reward provided by the PR <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, while also biasing the policy update towards regions in which the PR <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is accurate.
Our goal is thus</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}(s,a)]-\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)\,," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}(s,a)]-\gamma\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)\,,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyper-parameter and we use the BT loss <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math> of a PRs parameterized with <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> on actions sampled from <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, we cannot directly evaluate the BT loss <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>, as it requires pairwise comparisons for actions drawn from <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As we will show below, under some assumptions, overly sharp optima of the objective <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J(\phi,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(\phi,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> correspond to overly sharp maxima of the PR <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, which imply an excess BT loss <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}</annotation></semantics></math> of the PR.
Regularizing the policy gradient norm during training biases the optimization towards flat optima <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, avoiding this problem.
Instead of <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>, we thus use the policy gradient norm <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, yielding the practically optimizable</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\max_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}(s,a)]-\gamma\left\|\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)\right\|^{2}\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{\phi}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}(s,a)]-\gamma\left\|\nabla_{\phi}J(\phi,\theta)\right\|^{2}\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Gradient Regularization Improves Proxy Reward Accuracy</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our argument consists of three steps:
GR biases optimization towards flat maxima.
Flat maxima imply pairwise robust policies.
Pairwise robust policies correspond to accurate PRs, under the assumption of a flat reward.
We provide an illustration in <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview ‣ 3 Accurate Proxy Rewards via Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.
We note that our argument in this section focuses on continuous action spaces, while LMs use discrete action spaces.
We discuss this discrepancy at the end of this section and provide experimental evidence in the LM setting in <a href="#S4" title="4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4</span></a> and <a href="#S5" title="5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">GR Favors Flat Maxima in Parameter Space</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It is well known that GR favors flat minima in the parameter space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barrett and Dherin, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karakida et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
One way to see this is the argument of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2022)</a></cite>, connecting the gradient norm to Lipschitz continuity, which we reproduce for completeness in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Connection of Gradient Regularization and Lipschitz Continuity ‣ Appendix B Proof(s) ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.
It is also well known in the supervised learning literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997</a>)</cite> that flat minima lead to better generalization, i.e., a smaller difference between the population loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and the loss on the training set <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.
Equivalently, in RL, we would directly expect GR to ensure a similar PR score obtained on the training prompts <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{J}(\phi,\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim D_{\mathrm{tr}},a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>J</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>tr</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{J}(\phi,\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim D_{\mathrm{tr}},a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]</annotation></semantics></math> and on the test prompts <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J(\phi,\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim D_{\mathrm{te}},a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>te</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J(\phi,\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim D_{\mathrm{te}},a\sim\pi_{\phi}}[\widetilde{R}_{\theta}(s,a)]</annotation></semantics></math>.
Instead of considering generalization, we consider the PR accuracy, or more precisely the BT loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}</annotation></semantics></math>, necessitating the next two steps.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Flat Maxima in Parameter Space imply Robust Maxima in Action Space</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We need to connect the flatness of an optimum in parameter space with its flatness in action space, often referred to as robustness.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Yoon (2025)</a></cite> previously investigated this connection under the assumption of a ball with constant reward, which we use as starting point.
While they assume a constant return on a ball <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B(\phi^{*},\mathcal{E})\coloneq\{\epsilon:\|\epsilon\|\leq\mathcal{E}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B(\phi^{*},\mathcal{E})\coloneq\{\epsilon:\|\epsilon\|\leq\mathcal{E}\}</annotation></semantics></math> around the optimum <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, we allow the reward to decrease by at most <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{L}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}</annotation></semantics></math> flat reward maximum)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a reward function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> and policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>, parameterized by <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, a maximum <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}</annotation></semantics></math>-flat if the following holds:</p>
