<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also define the concept of a <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>-pairwise robust policy, which measures the probability of action pairs <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{1},a_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{1},a_{2})</annotation></semantics></math> sampled from the policy violating <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K/\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K/\delta</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz-continuity, i.e. <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\widetilde{R}(s,a_{1})-\widetilde{R}(s,a_{2})|&gt;K,\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|&lt;\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\widetilde{R}(s,a_{1})-\widetilde{R}(s,a_{2})|&gt;K,\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|&lt;\delta</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_definition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Definition 3.2</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(<math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>-pairwise robust policy)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}(a|s)" display="inline" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math>, define the sharpness set <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="S_{K,\delta}(R):=\{(s,a_{1},a_{2}):\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|\leq\delta,|R(s,a_{1})-R(s,a_{2})|&gt;K\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation A policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>-pairwise robust for a reward <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> if</p>

<p id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta}(R)|\pi_{\phi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta}(R)|\pi_{\phi})</annotation></semantics></math> being the probability under <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\sim P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\sim P(s)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{1},a_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\phi}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mover><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mover><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{1},a_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\pi_{\phi}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We obtain the following proposition, linking flatness in parameter space to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math> in action space, under the assumption of a <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>-smooth PR:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 3.3</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>( <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}</annotation></semantics></math> flat reward implies <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math> robust policy)<span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Assume a Gaussian policy with fixed covariance <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Sigma</annotation></semantics></math>, where we denote the policy noise <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)</annotation></semantics></math>, and that <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}(s,a)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}(s,a)</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>-smooth in <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>.
Further, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{J}(\phi^{*}):=\nabla_{\phi}\,\mu_{\phi}(s)\bigm|_{\phi=\phi^{*}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝔍</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><msub><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" stretchy="true">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{J}(\phi^{*}):=\nabla_{\phi}\,\mu_{\phi}(s)\bigm|_{\phi=\phi^{*}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Jacobian matrix of the mean action <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\phi}(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\phi}(s)</annotation></semantics></math>.
If <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is an <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo>−</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}-\widehat{L}</annotation></semantics></math> flat reward maximum, then the PR action gradient <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\nabla_{a}\widetilde{R}(s,\mu_{\phi}(s))\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>a</mi></msub><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>μ</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\nabla_{a}\widetilde{R}(s,\mu_{\phi}(s))\|</annotation></semantics></math> is bounded by</span></p>

<p id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">with radius <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{*}\leq\|\mathfrak{J}(\phi^{*})\|\,\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{E}^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi>𝔍</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{*}\leq\|\mathfrak{J}(\phi^{*})\|\,\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{E}^{2})</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a given <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K/\delta&gt;G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K/\delta&gt;G</annotation></semantics></math>, we then know that no pairwise violations can occur within the radius <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r:=\frac{1}{\beta}\bigl(\frac{K}{\delta}-G\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mi>δ</mi></mfrac><mo>−</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r:=\frac{1}{\beta}\bigl(\frac{K}{\delta}-G\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math>, and thus the policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.Thmtheorem3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>-robust with</span></p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta}(\widetilde{R})\mid\pi_{\phi^{*}})\leq 2\,P(\|Z\|&gt;r)\coloneq\rho\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≔</mo><mi>ρ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta}(\widetilde{R})\mid\pi_{\phi^{*}})\leq 2\,P(\|Z\|&gt;r)\coloneq\rho\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The proposition follows first linking flatness in parameter space to flatness in action space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee and Yoon, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Then, under a <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>-smooth PR, by a gradient bound we can ensure the absence of non-Lipschitz action pairs within a radius <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> around the mean.
Thus a violation requires at least one of the actions to fall outside this region <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pr(\|Z\|&gt;r)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Pr</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pr(\|Z\|&gt;r)</annotation></semantics></math> and the final results follows from a union bound.
A full derivation is shown in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Proof(s) ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.
Intuitively, for a given maximum, as the sensitivity to disturbances <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>L</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{L}</annotation></semantics></math> increases, the probability of overly sharp actions <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})</annotation></semantics></math> increases as well.
As the radius of the robustness <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> increases, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})</annotation></semantics></math> decreases or stays constant, as we can freely pick a smaller <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E^{\prime}&lt;E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>E</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E^{\prime}&lt;E</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, flatter, wider minima decrease the risk of sharp action pairs.
Next we will show that a larger <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})</annotation></semantics></math> incurs a larger excess BT loss <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p4.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Non-Robust Policies Imply Inaccurate Proxy Reward</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To connect <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\delta,K,\rho)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\delta,K,\rho)</annotation></semantics></math>-robustness and the BT loss, we make the assumption of an <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz true reward, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|R^{*}(s,a_{1})-R^{*}(s,a_{2})|\leq L\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|R^{*}(s,a_{1})-R^{*}(s,a_{2})|\leq L\|a_{1}-a_{2}\|</annotation></semantics></math>. We then obtain</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 3.4</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">For prompts <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s\sim P(s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s\sim P(s)</annotation></semantics></math>, pairs of actions <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{1},a_{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{1},a_{2})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz true reward function <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, proxy reward <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, policy <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K&gt;L\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&gt;L\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, the excess BT loss can be lower bounded as</span></p>
<table id="S3.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\widetilde{R})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(R^{*})\geq 2(\sigma(K)-\sigma(L\delta))^{2}P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\widetilde{R})-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(R^{*})\geq 2(\sigma(K)-\sigma(L\delta))^{2}P(S_{K,\delta}|\pi_{\phi})\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The proof is shown in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 BT-Loss Lower Bound Based on Sharpness ‣ Appendix B Proof(s) ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.
A non-robust policy in action space at least incurs an excess BT loss proportionate to the probability of overly sharp pairs <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta})</annotation></semantics></math> and the magnitude of the sharpness <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\sigma(K)-\sigma(L\delta))^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\sigma(K)-\sigma(L\delta))^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
By changing the policy <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> to decrease the ratio of violating pairs <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(S_{K,\delta})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(S_{K,\delta})</annotation></semantics></math> or the magnitude of the violations <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, we obtain a policy that induces a smaller excess BT loss.
As shown above, we can bias the policy updates towards such policies with GR.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Limitations</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While GR itself can be applied to LMs regardless of whether the action space <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is discrete or continuous, our theoretical argument assumes a Gaussian policy and requires a distance function, which is difficult to define for LMs.
As we assume the true reward to be Lipschitz under this distance, a distance under a representation that captures semantic closeness <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi(a):\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi(a):\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, such as the hidden space of the LM we are training, would be an appealing option.
For example in the illustrative Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a> (left), the distance in action corresponds to semantic similarity, not formatting.
Further, we only address excess BT loss incurred by overly sharp maxima, i.e. overly sharp PR maxima.
We do not show whether or not GR prevents convergence to flat but incorrect regions of the PR.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To empirically validate our theory, we next show that implicit GR, via Reference Resets, can improve RLHF. In <a href="#S5" title="5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 5</span></a> we leverage explicit GR for further improvements.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">When gradient norm decreases in a reset iteration, so do sharpness, and BT Loss <math id="S4.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>RM</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RM}}</annotation></semantics></math>.<span id="S4.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Evolution of reward, sharpness and BT loss during training on TL;DR with Pythia 1B using GRPO+reference resets, resets shown as grey dashed lines. After initially spiking in an iteration, gradient norm decreases along with the sharpness of the parameters and the BT-loss under the current policy. We show moving averages over 30 steps.

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Reference Resets outperform all possible weights <math id="S4.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> of KL penalty.<span id="S4.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Oracle evaluation (Gold Model Score) vs KL from initial model for Pythia 1B on the TL;DR test set.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Instead of performing explicit GR, we can rely on the implicit GR inherent to stochastic gradient descent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Barrett and Dherin, 2021</a>)</cite>. We propose to leverage Reference Resets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> where the KL penalty is changed by iteratively resetting its reference to the current policy <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\phi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\phi}</annotation></semantics></math> during training i.e., the update is penalized with <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\phi};\pi_{\phi^{\prime}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\phi};\pi_{\phi^{\prime}})</annotation></semantics></math>, where every <math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> steps we set <math id="S4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi^{\prime}\leftarrow\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mi>ϕ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi^{\prime}\leftarrow\phi</annotation></semantics></math>.
Since implicit GR usually occurs during the later stages of training, we find Reference Resets with a sufficient number of gradient steps per iteration to be an effective way of obtaining flat maxima.
While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025a)</a></cite> reset the policy when the reward has stagnated, we instead choose to perform resets every <math id="S4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> gradient steps similar to prior work using resets in RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nikishin et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Noukhovitch et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
We find that it is important to train beyond reward stagnation, as the gradient norm decreases significantly only after stagnation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We experiment on the well-known TL;DR summarization task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stiennon et al., 2020</a>)</cite> of Reddit posts with human summaries. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gao et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> we make this a controlled synthetic setup, where the preference and evaluation data is relabeled by a “gold” reward model, Skywork-RewardLlama-3.1-8B-v0.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Compared to noisy human preferences, this setup gives us an oracle that enables consistent evaluations. We run experiments with models from both Pythia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and Qwen 2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> families for different scales. See full details in Appendix <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 RLHF Details ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Gradient Norm Tracks Sharpness and RM Accuracy</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test our theory of GR, we plot the gradient norm against three important empirical values: 1) The training reward from the RM. 2) The sharpness of the current policy parameters <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math>, which we predict is tied to reward-hacking. The sharpness is estimated by sampling 32 perturbations <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{32}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>32</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{32}</annotation></semantics></math> and evaluating <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S(\phi,\theta)=\max_{i}J(\phi,\theta)-J(\phi+\epsilon_{i},\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S(\phi,\theta)=\max_{i}J(\phi,\theta)-J(\phi+\epsilon_{i},\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, for each checkpoint. And 3) the BT loss <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\theta,\phi)</annotation></semantics></math>, which represents how accurate our reward model is for our current policy. We sample completions from our model, label with the gold RM, and get the BT loss under our training RM. In this way, we can empirically check whether we are training in a regime where our PR is accurate.
We train a Pythia 1B model with GRPO+Reference Resets and show results in <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a> with dashed vertical lines representing resets.
In each iteration the gradient norm initially spikes and the reward increases quickly.
After the reward stabilizes, the gradient norm decreases. With it the sharpness of the parameters and the BT loss also decrease. This demonstrates that the gradient norm is tied to both the sharpness and accuracy of the PR.
Continuing training after the reset, we now start out with a more accurate RM. This enables training in a regime with a good PR, leading to a better final policy.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">

</span></div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reference Resets Outperform Standard KL</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run an extensive comparison across both families and two sizes per model on standard baselines.
The initial models are SFT-trained on TLDR data.
From there we compare our method to DPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, DPO with reference reset, also known as Trust Region DPO (TR-DPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gorbatovski et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and standard GRPO with a fixed KL penalty.
Our results are shown in <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Gradient Norm Tracks Sharpness and RM Accuracy ‣ 4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>.
GRPO + Reference Resets strongly outperforms all other methods for all but one setup.
Notably, a Pythia 1B model trained with Reference Resets performs better than a Pythia 2.8B model trained with standard GRPO, even with a finely-tuned <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, as shown in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
In our experiments, TR-DPO’s Reference Resets do not seem to afford the same performance improvements.
We speculate that this is because DPO does not use an RM, thus there can be no sharp action-space PR maxima which GR would help to avoid.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Is a Scheduled or Weaker <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> a Sufficient Alternative?</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Originally, Reference Resets were proposed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> not to improve RM accuracy but to prevent the KL term from dominating the reward sum.
If this was their main mechanism, decreasing the strength of the KL penalty <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> should have a similar effect.
Further, an analysis of the optimal policy under iterated KL constrained optimization (see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Reference Resets in RLHF ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>) shows that the optimal policy for <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> reset iterations is equivalent to the optimal policy with a KL constraint to <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{1}</annotation></semantics></math> with a lower penalty strength <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\prime}=\beta/i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{\prime}=\beta/i</annotation></semantics></math>.
However, <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a> shows that decreasing <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is not able to match Reference Resets.
This demonstrates the necessity for our novel insight that Reference Resets change the optimization dynamics via implicit gradient regularization during training and its effects on the PR accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Explicit Gradient Regularization</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reference Resets are an indirect way of regularizing the gradient norm, require many more gradient steps, and do not provide a direct, controllable way to trade-off reward maximization, adherence to the initial policy, and gradient regularization.
We therefore propose a novel application of explicit GR methods to RLHF and RLVR, specifically finite-difference GR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karakida et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
To improve training stability, we implement parameter perturbations only on the transformer blocks, leaving the embedding layer and output head untouched, and clip the intermediate gradients.
To make GR training efficient, we reuse the actions <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\sim\pi_{\phi}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\sim\pi_{\phi}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> to calculate both the gradients <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla J(\phi,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>J</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla J(\phi,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\nabla J(\phi+\varepsilon\nabla J(\phi,\theta),\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla J(\phi+\varepsilon\nabla J(\phi,\theta),\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>.
In principle, this would require new actions <math id="S5.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a\sim\pi_{\phi+\varepsilon\nabla J(\phi,\theta)}(a|s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ε</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\sim\pi_{\phi+\varepsilon\nabla J(\phi,\theta)}(a|s)</annotation></semantics></math> or correction by importance sampling. However, we empirically found this to be unnecessary and reusing actions reduces computation overhead.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          In our MATH reasoning experiments on 8 GH200 GPUs, generating the actions took on average 7.4s, while the policy update took 60ms without GR and 150ms with GR.</span></span></span>
PyTorch-style pseudocode, implementation details and experimental details are shown in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>GR Mitigates Hacking Reward Models in RLHF</h3>

<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">

</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first investigate whether GR can fully replace the standard KL penalty in RLHF.
Scaling up from TL;DR, we run experiments on the AlpacaFarm dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dubois et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, with preference feedback from GPT 4.1-Nano.
We again evaluate with winrate: generating completions on the test set and judging them against reference completions with GPT4.1-Nano.
We train models from the Qwen 2.5 family, running for 1000 gradient steps in the 1.5B experiments and 500 gradient steps in the 0.5B and 3B experiments and early-stop based on the training winrate.
We evaluate and ablate GR in four settings: 1) no KL penalty, no GR 2) KL penalty, 3) Reference Resets + KL, 4) GR without KL.
We do a grid-search to find the optimal strength for each regularization method for each model size and show results in <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.1 GR Mitigates Hacking Reward Models in RLHF ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>.
In most cases using RL without regularization only yields a modest improvement over the initial SFT policy. RL with a KL penalty works decently well though
Reference Resets is sometimes better. But explicit GR consistently performs best, demonstrating that it can replace the KL penalty and improve overall performance.</p>
</div>

The x-axis scale is nonlinear.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Explicit GR is robust to RM accuracy</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">RLHF performance can vary heavily depending on the accuracy of the RM and performance of the initial policy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
To demonstrate robustness, we rerun our whole pipeline two more times for the 1.5B model: initial SFT, dataset sampling, RM training, GRPO with hyper-parameter tuning.
In <a href="#S5.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 5.1 GR Mitigates Hacking Reward Models in RLHF ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 5</span></a> we show the winrate of each trained model against the accuracy of the RM with which it trained.
We observe that GR performs significantly better than Reference Resets or a KL penalty when the RM is weaker, demonstrating better robustness. Reference Resets do perform slightly better than GR with the strongest RM, where reward-hacking is less prevalent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also find that GR is robust to choices of hyper-parameters <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, and show a learning rate sweep in Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Gradient Regularization 𝛾, 𝜀, and learning rate sweeps ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.
Finally, we discover that strong GR can even compensate in robustness for a weak RM by training in a regime where the RM is more accurate than on its training distribution, see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 Gradient regularization decreases BT loss ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>GR Prevents Focus on Easy Rule-Based Rewards</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work in RLVR has generally removed the KL penalty to allow for a stronger deviation from the base model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-4.5 Team et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olmo Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, though others have kept it for training stability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kimi Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
As GR does not constrain the divergence from the base model, but may provide the desired training stability, we investigate whether it can be used in RLVR to enable more flexibility while preventing reward hacking.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S5.F6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GR prevents overly focusing on formatting reward.<span id="S5.F6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Qwen2.5-0.5B on GSM8K, test set accuracy (left) and formatting reward (right), the dashed line shows the optimal formatting reward. Without regularization, the policy focuses overly on the formatting reward, resulting in worse accuracy.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We perform experiments with Qwen 2.5 0.5B-Instruct and 1.5B-Instruct on GSM8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cobbe et al., 2021</a>)</cite> with the standard combination of formatting and correctness reward, see full details in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.
We indeed observe more stable training and improved final accuracy, as shown in <a href="#S5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 GR Prevents Focus on Easy Rule-Based Rewards ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 6</span></a> (left) and <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 GR Prevents Focus on Easy Rule-Based Rewards ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>.
Notably, improved performance comes at the expense of a slightly worse adherence to the formatting reward.
In the presence of both rewards, we can see the excessive focus on the easier formatting reward as a kind of reward hacking, even when neither reward is hackable on its own.
This demonstrates how GR can be effective in situations with a combination of rule-based rewards.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S5.T4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GR prevents focus on easy questions.<span id="S5.T4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Accuracy on MATH with rule-based reward, by difficulty of the question category, grouped by base-model accuracy. Colored depending on <span id="S5.T4.7.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#2CA02C;">increase</span> or <span id="S5.T4.7.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#D62728;">decrease</span> after Step 250. </table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we show that a form of reward hacking is also possible even within a single reward and how GR can mitigate it. We train a Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct model with a rule-based reward on MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
The base model achieves 46.3% pass@1 accuracy and GRPO+GR (57.6%) clearly outperforms standard GRPO (54.8%).
In order to discern reward hacking, we investigate the accuracy more closely. We divide performance into quintiles of difficulty so that test-set questions are split based on the initial accuracy of their category and level-labels, as provided by the dataset
As shown in <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.2 GR Prevents Focus on Easy Rule-Based Rewards ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 4</span></a>,
without regularization the performance on the easiest quintile of questions continues to improve past 250 steps. But after the first 250 steps, performance on harder questions actually degrades. This demonstrates how RL can focus on learning only the easiest questions in order to hack even a rule-based reward.
In contrast, training with GR more evenly improves the accuracies across difficulties, avoiding the focus on the easier questions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S5.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S5.F7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GR prevents reward hacking with LLM-as-a-Judge<span id="S5.F7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Results when training Qwen2.5-0.5B-Inst. on GSM8K with Qwen2.5 1.5B-Inst. as judge. Left: LLM-Judge and rule-based accuracy over time, showing reward hacking without regularization.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we investigate RL with LLM-as-a-Judge.
As LLM-as-a-Judge can be susceptible to adversarial attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we presume it can also be reward-hacked as a PR.
To investigate, we re-run the previous GSM8k experiments but replace the rule-based correctness reward with an LLM judge based on Qwen2.5 1.5B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
The judge receives the problem description, true answer, model response, model reasoning, and is instructed to output a score for correctness (1 to 5) which acts as the reward.
As shown in <a href="#S5.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 GR Mitigates Hacking LLM-as-a-Judge in RLVR ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 7</span></a>, without regularization the model quickly starts to “hack” the judge LLM. LLM judge score goes sharply up while pass@1 accuracy on the test set peaks quite early. Empirically, we observed the model outputting excessive brackets and new HTML tags to fool the judge. In contrast, both GR and KL show much more reasonable train rewards and prevent excessive reward hacking. But as shown in
<a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 GR Prevents Focus on Easy Rule-Based Rewards ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>, GR results in better final performance.
Confirming results in <a href="#S4" title="4 Reference Reset as Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section 4</span></a>, we also see that, without regularization, an increase in gradient norm occurs when reward hacking begins, shown in <a href="#S5.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 5.3 GR Mitigates Hacking LLM-as-a-Judge in RLVR ‣ 5 Explicit Gradient Regularization ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 8</span></a> (left).
In <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 LLM judge ablation ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a> we compare different judge models, showing that the additional cost of GR can be amortized by allowing the usage of smaller judge models.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have investigated the problem of RL with proxy rewards (PR) and proposed a novel perspective: learning a policy in a regime where the PR is accurate.
For this purpose, we have derived a theoretical connection between the flatness of an optimum and the Bradley-Terry loss of the PR at this optimum.
By regularizing the gradient norm during training, we can bias the RL updates towards such a flat optimum.
We first validated our theoretical analysis by using implicit gradient regularization (GR) via Reference Resets, showing they improve upon a KL penalty.
We then proposed to use explicit GR based on an efficient implementation of a finite-difference estimate.
Explicit GR allows us to mitigate reward model hacking of RMs in RLHF, reduce focus on easy rule-based rewards in RLVR, and alleviate format hacking with LLM-as-a-judge.
We believe that GR is a promising candidate to completely replace KL penalties and improve training runs that currently eschew regularization.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Acknowledgements</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We would like to thank Soichiro Nishimori and Thanawat Lodkaew for helpful discussions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a method to prevent reward hacking in RL post-training of LLMs.
We believe that preventing reward hacking is likely to have a beneficial impact in general.
However, our theory only considers certain specific kinds of reward hacking, thus there is a risk that by overly relying on our method, users may miss other kinds of reward hacking, which should be monitored independently.</p>
</div>
</section>
