<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the hyperparameters as stated in Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ C.4 Reasoning Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ C.4 Reasoning Experiments ‣ Appendix C Experiment Details ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.
We did not tune <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and simply used conservative values from the RLHF experiments.
For both GR and no regularization we tried learning rates <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A3.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\times 10^{-6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>6</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times 10^{-6}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For GR, the larger learning rate was beneficial.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We follow the setup of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2025)</a></cite>, with GSM8K using one-shot prompting, math uses chain-of-thought prompting, both with the default Qwen2.5-Instruct system instructions.
We also use the same reward terms, which are based on the rewards used by Open R1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hugging Face, 2025</a>)</cite>.
For GSM8K, the prompt is <code id="A3.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">Respond in the following format: &lt;reasoning&gt;...&lt;/reasoning&gt;&lt;answer&gt;...&lt;/answer&gt;</code>, followed by a one-shot example.
The reward consists of a rule-based correctness reward (<math id="A3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,2]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,2]</annotation></semantics></math>), a formatting term checking whether the answer is an integer formatting reward (<math id="A3.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,0.5\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,0.5\}</annotation></semantics></math>), a formatting term checking whether the formatting is exactly followed including whitespace (<math id="A3.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>), and excluding whitespace (<math id="A3.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,1.0\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1.0</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,1.0\}</annotation></semantics></math>), and a formatting reward for matching XML tags (<math id="A3.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,0.5\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,0.5\}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On MATH the prompt is simply the problem statement followed by <code id="A3.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">Let's think step by step and output the</code> <code id="A3.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">final answer within \\boxed{}.</code>.
The used reward consists of a correctness reward (<math id="A3.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,2]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,2]</annotation></semantics></math>) and a formatting reward rewarding up to three of the following with <math id="A3.SS4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/3</annotation></semantics></math> each: <span id="A3.SS4.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Step #</span> keywords, Numbered lists, bullet points, <span id="A3.SS4.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">First, Second, Next, Finally</span> keywords.
This is done to encourage reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hugging Face, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">

<p id="A3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main text we use Qwen2.5 1.5B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as a judge with the following prompt:</p>

</span><span id="lstnumberx57.19" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">you</span><span id="lstnumberx57.20" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx57.21" class="ltx_text id="lstnumberx57.49" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">trace</span>.
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally use 1-shot prompting with a correct example.
During training the agent is provided the correctness score scaled to <math id="A3.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,2]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,2]</annotation></semantics></math>, along with the same formatting rewards used in the rule-based-reward setting.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Additional Experiments</h2>

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Gradient Regularization <math id="A4.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, and learning rate sweeps</h3>

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A4.F11" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:103.5pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/grVSrmLoss.svg" id="A4.SS1.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:143/107;" width="143" height="107"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 11</span>: </span><span id="A4.F11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Strong GR can decrease BT loss below initial value.<span id="A4.F11.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> BT loss <math id="A4.F11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\phi,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\phi,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> during training of a Qwen 2.5 0.5B model on the TL;DR task with GR, using the Gold reward model.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<figure id="A4.SS1.fig6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A4.SS1.fig4" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:155.3pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/gradreg_lr_sweep_gpt1_5B.svg" id="A4.SS1.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:150/129;" width="150" height="129"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.SS1.fig4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 12</span>: </span><span id="A4.SS1.fig4.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Learning rate sweep for KL penalty and GR when training a Qwen 2.5-1.5B model on the Alpacafarm dataset. KL <math id="A4.SS1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>, GR <math id="A4.SS1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=3\times 10^{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=3\times 10^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math></span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A4.F13" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:155.3pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/judge_ablation.svg" id="A4.SS1.g5" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:150/128;" width="150" height="128"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 13</span>: </span><span id="A4.F13.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">GR allows usage of cheaper judges to reach same performance.<span id="A4.F13.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Test accuracy when training a Qwen2.5-0.5B model on GSM8K with different judges.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the sensitivity of GR to the hyper-parameters controlling strength of the regularization <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and the strength of the perturbation <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ε</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, we performed experiments on the Qwen2.5 1.5B model in the Alpaca GPT4.1 Nano setting.
We fix either <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=3\times 10^{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=3\times 10^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> and vary the respective other parameter.
We show the results in Figure <a href="#A4.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ D.1 Gradient Regularization 𝛾, 𝜀, and learning rate sweeps ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.
We find the performance to be rather predictable, facilitating hyper-parameter tuning.
We used the same disturbance strength <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon=10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ε</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon=10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> for all experiments and did not find it necessary to tune it per task or model.
In the reasoning experiments we did not tune <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and simply used <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>, however, in the RLHF experiments we found it necessary to tune <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> as described above, just like we found it necessary to tune <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> for the KL penalty.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also perform a learning rate sweep for the KL penalty and GR in the same Alpaca, Qwen2.5 1.5B setting.
We use the best performing KL hyper-parameters from our main hyper-parameter optimization, i.e. <math id="A4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.1</annotation></semantics></math> for the KL penalty and <math id="A4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.03</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=0.03</annotation></semantics></math> for GR.
The results are shown in <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Gradient Regularization 𝛾, 𝜀, and learning rate sweeps ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>Gradient regularization decreases BT loss</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also perform experiments in the synthetic TL;DR gold model setup, training a Qwen 2.5 0.5B model with different GR strengths <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>.
The results in Figure <a href="#A4.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ D.1 Gradient Regularization 𝛾, 𝜀, and learning rate sweeps ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> show that stronger regularization leads to a lower BT model loss <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\phi,\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}(\phi,\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, evaluated on 4096 action pairs with labels from the gold reward model.
Interestingly, training with strong GR can result in a decreasing BT loss <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}</annotation></semantics></math> beyond the initial BT loss, which we did not observe when utilizing either KL regularization or Reference Resets.
This illustrates the practical strength of the connection between gradient norm and PR accuracy.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>LLM judge ablation</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the main text we are using Qwen2.5 1.5B-Instruct as judge.
As we are using similarly sized policy models, we believe this could be a useful proxy for experiments in which LLMs are trained with equally large judge models.
However, to see whether GR is also useful with comparatively stronger judges, we additionally run experiments with Qwen2.5 3B-Instruct and Qwen3 4B Instruct-2507 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> as judges.
We train a Qwen2.5 0.5B-Instruct model on GSM8K.
For Qwen3 we use <code id="A4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter">Judgement:... Correctness_score:... Coherence_score:...</code> as reply format instead of the xml tags, as we found Qwen3 to perform better with this format.
As shown in <a href="#A4.F13" title="In D.1 Gradient Regularization 𝛾, 𝜀, and learning rate sweeps ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, GR enables us to reach the same performance using a cheaper judge, potentially saving total computational cost.
In our setup with 8 GH200 GPUs, training with GR and the 1.5B judge took 84 minutes, while training without GR and the 4B judge took 88 minutes.
The additional cost of GR can thus be amortized by being able to use a cheaper judge.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.4 </span>KL penalty schedule</h3>

<figure id="A4.F14" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/sched_kl_div_gold.svg" id="A4.SS4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:177/177;" width="177" height="177"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/ResetSweepKLvsGoldScore.svg" id="A4.SS4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:221/177;" width="221" height="177"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A4.F14.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="A4.F14.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pythia 1B on TL;DR task. Left: Reference Resets schedule ablation. A scheduled <math id="A4.F14.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> performs better than a constant value, however, it does not match the performance of full Reference Resets.
Right: Steps per reset <math id="A4.F14.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> for GRPO + Reference Resets. A larger R is generally beneficial, but requires significantly more gradient steps.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While we have shown in the main text that Reference Resets perform better in RLHF than simply decreasing the strength of the KL penalty <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> from the beginning, another hypothesis might be that decreasing the KL strength <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> during training will match the results of Reference Resets.
As an additional baseline, we thus decrease the strength of the KL penalty to <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\prime}=\beta/i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{\prime}=\beta/i</annotation></semantics></math> in iteration <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, while keeping the reference as <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus in each iteration the optimal policy under Reference Resets and the scheduled <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> is the same, assuming the previous iterations converged to their respective optimal policies.
As shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ D.4 KL penalty schedule ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> (left), the schedule indeed yields a notable improvement over a fixed <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, but also does not match the performance of Reference Resets.
We attribute this to the KL penalty explicitly keeping the policy close to the good region of the RM found in previous iteration, which a scheduled <math id="A4.SS4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> does not ensure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.5 </span>Steps per reset <math id="A4.SS5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="A4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our theoretical derivation suggests that flatter minimum corresponds to a more accurate reward model.
Experiments show that the gradient norm keeps decreasing within each iteration even after the PR score is saturated.
Thus, we expect training for more steps <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> per reset to improve performance at the cost of a higher computational expense.
We evaluate different values for <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> when training a Pythia 1B model on the summarization task and show the results in Figure <a href="#A4.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ D.4 KL penalty schedule ‣ Appendix D Additional Experiments ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> (right), training each model for 1500 total steps.
Indeed, we find more steps <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> to lead to a better KL-Gold-Reward tradeoff and perhaps a better asymptotic reward.
However, for high values such as <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=400" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>400</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=400</annotation></semantics></math> the computational cost becomes prohibitively expensive, such that we use <math id="A4.SS5.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=200</annotation></semantics></math> in experiments unless otherwise specified.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.6 </span>Reward hacking example</h3>

<div id="A4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An example output by a Qwen2.5 0.5B model trained without regularization hacking a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct judge:</p>
<div id="A4.SS6.p1.2" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_language_text ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>

</div>

</div>

</span>100}}))))))))))))))))))))))))))))))&gt;&gt;
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx62" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx62.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">To</span><span id="lstnumberx62.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">find</span><span id="lstnumberx62.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">the</span><span id="lstnumberx62.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">final</span><span id="lstnumberx62.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">amount</span>,<span id="lstnumberx62.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">we</span><span id="lstnumberx62.12" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.13" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">perform</span><span id="lstnumberx62.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.15" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">the</span><span id="lstnumberx62.16" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.17" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">following</span><span id="lstnumberx62.18" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span><span id="lstnumberx62.19" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">steps</span>:
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx63" class="ltx_listingline">\[
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx64" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx64.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space">    </span>\<span id="lstnumberx64.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">text</span>{<span id="lstnumberx64.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">final_left</span>}}<span id="lstnumberx64.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>=<span id="lstnumberx64.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>500<span id="lstnumberx64.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>-<span id="lstnumberx64.7" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>100<span id="lstnumberx64.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>+<span id="lstnumberx64.9" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>100<span id="lstnumberx64.10" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>=<span id="lstnumberx64.11" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space"> </span>119}}
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx65" class="ltx_listingline">\))
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx66" class="ltx_listingline">&lt;/<span id="lstnumberx66.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">code</span>&gt;&gt;
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx67" class="ltx_listingline">&lt;/<span id="lstnumberx67.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">p</span>&gt;&gt;
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx68" class="ltx_listingline">&lt;/<span id="lstnumberx68.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">reasoning</span>&gt;
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx69" class="ltx_listingline">&lt;<span id="lstnumberx69.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">answer</span>&gt;
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx70" class="ltx_listingline">119
</div>
<div id="lstnumberx71" class="ltx_listingline">&lt;/<span id="lstnumberx71.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier">answer</span>&gt;
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Reference Resets in RLHF</h2>

<figure id="A5.F15" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18037v1/reset_vs_grpo_overview.svg" id="A5.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/159;" width="476" height="159"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F15.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 15</span>: </span><span id="A5.F15.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Proxy and gold reward for no resets (blue, <math id="A5.F15.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.06" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.06</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.06</annotation></semantics></math>) and resets (orange, <math id="A5.F15.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.3</annotation></semantics></math>). The proxy reward should thus match after 5 resets which here with <math id="A5.F15.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=200</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to 1200 training steps. The achieved proxy reward is relatively similar at training step <math id="A5.F15.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1200" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1200</annotation></semantics></math>, however, the gold reward with resets is significantly higher.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To investigate the impact of reference resets in RLHF we provide an asymptotic argument, showing an equivalence between using reference resets and using a lower <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.
While we show that this equivalence indeed shows up in experiments for the RM reward <math id="A5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>, the achieved true reward <math id="A5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> is significantly higher when doing reference sets than when using a lower <math id="A5.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.
This can not be explained by the asymptotic argument, we thus continue by providing an analysis from the point of view of optimization dynamics.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Asymptotic analysis</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It is well known (e.g. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al., 2023</a>, Appendix A.1)</cite>) that the optimal solution of the KL-regularized optimization problem <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\arg\max_{\pi}\widetilde{R}(s,a)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi,\pi^{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>π</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>KL</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\arg\max_{\pi}\widetilde{R}(s,a)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi,\pi^{1})</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>
<table id="A5.E30" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E30.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi(s,a)\propto\pi^{1}(s,a)\exp\left(\beta^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi(s,a)\propto\pi^{1}(s,a)\exp\left(\beta^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(30)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">With reference resets, we are solving this problem repeatedly, thus for iteration <math id="A5.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math></p>
<table id="A5.E31" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{k}(s,a)\propto\pi^{k-1}(s,a)\exp\left(\beta^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{k}(s,a)\propto\pi^{k-1}(s,a)\exp\left(\beta^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(31)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">If we insert <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{k-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{k-1}</annotation></semantics></math> into this, we obtain</p>
<table id="A5.E32" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.E32.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{k}(s,a)\propto\pi^{1}(s,a)\exp\left((\beta/k)^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{k}(s,a)\propto\pi^{1}(s,a)\exp\left((\beta/k)^{-1}\widetilde{R}(s,a)\right)\,.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(32)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Therefore, the optimal policy for Reference Resets with <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> iterations and KL-penalty strength <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> should be the same as the solution without resets with a weaker KL-penalty weight <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta^{\prime}=\beta/k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta^{\prime}=\beta/k</annotation></semantics></math>.
In experiments, we can indeed see a similar behavior when only looking at the RM reward, as shown in Figure <a href="#A5.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix E Reference Resets in RLHF ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> (left).
There, after 1200 steps the RM reward <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{R}</annotation></semantics></math> achieved with reset is roughly in the rang of reward without reference resets.
As this argument makes no statements about the true reward <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>R</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, we might expect it to be similar for both methods as well.
Surprisingly, we instead find that the true reward achieved by Reference Resets is significantly higher than the true reward achieved in a single stage.
We believe this effect can not be explained by an asymptotic analysis, thus motivating our optimization dynamics argument.
In Figure <a href="#A5.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Appendix E Reference Resets in RLHF ‣ Gradient Regularization Prevents Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> (right), we also show that using Reference Resets higher gold reward regions can be obtained for the same RM BT loss <math id="A5.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>BT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
